newsitem.title: FRANCE: All 14 Moslems held in French bomb raids freed.
newsitem.headline: All 14 Moslems held in French bomb raids freed.

text.p: French police released on Wednesday the last of 14 people seized in raids on Algerian Moslem targets around Paris, a week after a bomb on a Paris train killed four people.

Police said the last two people detained after dawn raids on Tuesday for questioning in a probe into last year's bomb attacks by Algerian Moslem militants were released on Wednesday morning with police apparently having little to show.
The other 12 were released on Tuesday after police found neither arms nor explosives in their flats in Paris and surrounding suburbs.

At a cabinet meeting, President Jacques Chirac praised the "coolness and sense of solidarity" shown by French citizens since last week's bomb killed four people and injured almost 100, government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said.
Seventeen people were still in hospital on Wednesday.
No group has claimed responsibility for the rush-hour blast.
Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre said the probe was going on in "satisfactory conditions" and praised cooperation with countries including Germany, Britain, Italy and Spain.

Debre's tough-talking predecessor Charles Pasqua on Sunday accused Germany, Britain and Belgium of offering immunity to Islamic guerrilla groups in exchange for promises not to operate in their territories.

Police said Tuesday's raids were not directly linked to the probe into last week's bomb. But the blast on the train at the Port-Royal station bore striking similarities to a series of attacks in 1995 that killed eight and injured more than 160.

Investigators say they suspect the Algerian Armed Islamic Group (GIA), which claimed responsibility for last year's bombs, also planted last week's bomb. The group accuses France of backing Algiers' military government in a war against the GIA.
Lamassoure quoted Debre as telling a cabinet meeting that "the investigation was being carried out in satisfactory, particularly active conditions, (and that) 160 people have been questioned."
He also quoted Debre as "insisting on the quality of cooperation with the foreign services of our European neighbours, especially Germany, Britain, Italy and Spain."
"We are working permanently with them and in real time," Debre told the cabinet, saying the cooperation had brought results. He gave no details.
The daily Le Monde said counter-intelligence services had sent Chirac's office a note 14 days before last week's bombing warning of a possible resumption of guerrilla attacks in France.
It said the one-page note was the final stage of an almost permanent alert in place since 1995.

Secret services had also warned in recent months of GIA members in Germany planning to enter France and of four GIA members in Italy who had abandoned a plan to plant a bomb in France before November 28, it said.
Meanwhile, a Senate committee approved a change in French law that would allow police to make night-time raids in anti-terrorist probes.
Currently, swoops have to be after 6 a.m. (0500 GMT). The full Senate and the National Assembly would have to approve the change before it could become law.

Investigators said the raids targeted a network alleged to be run by Ahmed Zaoui, former European leader of the GIA who was given a suspended four-year jail sentence by a Belgian court in November 1995.
